content.title: About
content.content: A custard-filled doughnut is a ring‑shaped fried or baked pastry made from wheat flour, sugar, eggs, milk and yeast, filled with a sweet custard made from eggs, sugar and milk, often flavored with vanilla.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Doughnuts appeared in Europe in the 19th century, and custard fillings became popular in the United States in the early 20th century.
Custard fillings are often thickened with corn starch, which makes them more stable for storage.
In Japan there is a version of the doughnut with custard, glazed and sprinkled with sea salt.
Custard‑filled doughnuts are frequently served in cafés as a “coffee companion” because of their sweet yet light flavor.
Gluten‑free versions exist, using rice or almond flour instead of wheat.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates and a modest amount of fat provide quick energy.

items.title: Calcium from dairy
items.content: The milk‑based custard supplies calcium important for bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and yeast in the dough contribute B1, B2 and B6 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: Small amount of protein
items.content: Eggs add protein, which helps tissue repair.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The custard contains milk, which may trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Trans fats from frying
items.content: Deep‑frying can create trans fats, which are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Doughnuts are calorie‑dense; moderate consumption is advised for weight‑watching individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve custard‑filled doughnuts slightly warm; they can be enjoyed as a standalone dessert or paired with coffee, tea, or a milkshake. Optional toppings include powdered sugar or cinnamon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate for up to 5 days; bring to room temperature before eating.
